clinicalPearls: Precocious puberty is conventionally defined as the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before about 8 years in girls and 9 years in boys.

It is broadly classified as central (gonadotropin-dependent, from early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis) or peripheral (gonadotropin-independent, from sex steroids produced outside the normal axis).
Central precocious puberty is far more common in girls and is usually idiopathic, whereas in boys an underlying CNS lesion is more likely and must be excluded.
Accelerated linear growth and advanced bone age are typical; paradoxically, premature epiphyseal fusion can compromise final adult height.
A GnRH (or GnRH-agonist) stimulation test helps distinguish central from peripheral causes by assessing the gonadotropin response.
Isolated premature thelarche or premature adrenarche are usually benign normal variants but should be monitored to ensure they are not the start of true precocity.
Peripheral causes include congenital adrenal hyperplasia, gonadal or adrenal tumours, McCune-Albright syndrome, and exogenous sex steroid exposure.
Beyond physical changes, early puberty can carry psychosocial consequences that warrant support for the child and family.
reference.pathophysiology: In central precocious puberty the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis reactivates prematurely, with pulsatile GnRH secretion stimulating pituitary gonadotropins and subsequent gonadal sex steroid production, reproducing normal but early puberty. In peripheral precocious puberty sex steroids arise independently of GnRH from the gonads, adrenals, tumours, or exogenous sources, producing secondary sexual characteristics without central axis activation. Sex steroids accelerate growth and skeletal maturation, so advanced bone age can ultimately limit final height.
additionalDifferentials: Premature adrenarche (early pubic/axillary hair without other puberty)
CNS lesion (hamartoma, tumour, prior irradiation, or injury)
additionalInvestigations: Basal and GnRH-stimulated LH and FSH
Adrenal androgens and 17-hydroxyprogesterone when a peripheral cause is suspected
Pelvic ultrasound in girls to assess ovarian and uterine development
MRI of the brain, particularly in boys or where a central lesion is suspected
redFlags: Neurological signs, headaches, or visual disturbance suggesting an intracranial lesion
Rapidly progressive virilisation or a palpable abdominal/gonadal mass suggesting a hormone-secreting tumour
Precocious puberty in a boy, which more often has a serious underlying cause
Very early or rapidly advancing puberty threatening severe height compromise
Cafe-au-lait macules with bony abnormalities suggesting McCune-Albright syndrome
reference.prognosis: Idiopathic central precocious puberty generally has a good outcome, and appropriate treatment can preserve growth potential and address psychosocial concerns; prognosis in secondary forms depends on the underlying cause, such as a CNS lesion or hormone-secreting tumour.
pitfalls: Assuming precocious puberty is idiopathic in a boy without imaging to exclude a CNS lesion
Confusing benign premature thelarche or adrenarche with true central precocity
Overlooking the impact of advanced bone age on final adult height
Neglecting the psychosocial needs of a child developing ahead of peers
management: Central precocious puberty: GnRH-agonist therapy to suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, halt pubertal progression and preserve adult height

Peripheral precocious puberty: treat the source, with glucocorticoids for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, aromatase inhibitors or anti-androgens to block sex-steroid effects, and surgical removal of a hormone-secreting tumour
Identify and manage any causative central nervous system lesion, particularly in boys
Remove exogenous sex-steroid exposure where identified
Monitor growth velocity, bone age and pubertal staging to gauge treatment response and predicted height
Psychological support for the child and family regarding early physical and emotional changes
Specialist paediatric endocrinology referral, with neurosurgical or oncology input where relevant
